summary:
Ad Astra is a browser game for kids aged 7 to 12. You command a small base on the Moon or on Mars with a crew of four, one day at a time. Each day you choose who does which job: grow lettuce, make air, fix the water recycler, go outside for science, or add moon soil to the shelter wall. 

Real NASA data sets the conditions. This week's real solar flares from NASA DONKI decide how big the solar storms are. NASA OSDR RadLab measurements of the May 2024 storm size the radiation. NASA JPL planet positions give today's real radio delay to Mars, so a question to Earth takes about 20 minutes to be answered and the base cannot wait.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Ad Astra turns the challenge into a base you run yourself. Kids pick a mission (three on the Moon, two on Mars), then play day by day: tap an astronaut, tap a room, and that astronaut works there. At the end of the day the simulation shows what happened to the battery, the air, the water, the food and the radiation dose. Zooming into a room shows the crew working in it, and finishing a job can open a short mini-game (a memory game in the lab, fixing pipes, harvesting lettuce, sorting rock samples, opening valves in order, calm breathing in the shelter). Winning one gives a small bonus. The game works without them.

REAL DATA, NOT INVENTED

- NASA DONKI (live): this week's real solar flares set the size of the solar storms, and the warnings name the biggest real flare.

- NASA OSDR RadLab: BioSentinel (deep space) and Curiosity RAD (Mars) measurements of the May 2024 storm size the radiation.

- NASA JPL "Approximate Positions of the Planets": today's Earth–Mars radio delay and today's Mars–Sun distance, which sets the power of the Mars solar panels.

- NASA OSDR studies (bone, muscle, bed rest, lettuce on the Space Station) appear as facts in the rooms.

- NASA Mars Trek places the Mars base in Jezero Crater.

Every number is either traced to a source or labeled "game rule", and the in-game sources screen lists them all. Archived data is never shown as live.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

Kids learn by making trade-offs, not by reading: if they skip the shelter, the storm pauses the mission and the game explains why and how to do better. The radio part lets them guess how long Earth takes to answer, then watch the signal cross space. Teachers can give the whole class the same mission code, so everyone plays the same storm.

DESIGN FOR 7 TO 12

Short sentences, big buttons, a read-aloud button on every message, a colour-blind-safe palette, and no account. The player's name and progress stay in the browser; nothing is sent anywhere.

TOOLS

Plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript (no framework, works offline and on Chromebooks), Canvas 2D for the base, the first-person cutscenes and the mini-games, the Web Audio API for sound, and a deterministic simulation checked by automatic robot players (every mission must be winnable).

Pixel art made with PixelLab (AI), marked "AI" in the game.

Code written with the help of Claude (AI). Code license Apache-2.0, art CC BY 4.0.

Source: https://github.com/halvgud/adastra
